source.title: Structure-Enhanced Protein Instruction Tuning: Towards General-Purpose Protein Understanding with LLMs
source.authors: Wei Wu; Chao Wang; Li-Yi Chen; Ming-Ze Yin; Yiheng Zhu; Kun Fu; Jie-Ping Ye; Hui Xiong; Zheng Wang

record.file_problem: The full paper and appendices are present. Some table content is flattened in the supplied text, so individual scores for the instruction-tuned size comparison cannot be safely matched to models and metrics.
record.tranche_reason: The paper compares downstream protein-task performance across language models of different stated sizes and explicitly discusses scaling, but it does not measure pretraining loss or reproduce the original language-model scaling experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Kaplan et al.'s scaling laws as motivation and reports downstream task comparisons. It does not test held-out pretraining loss, small-run extrapolation, compute-optimal parameter/token allocation, architecture effects at fixed parameter count, other modalities as scaling-law tests, or fit dependence. Other cited scaling-law results are not recorded as findings of this study.
record.test_reason: This is only a weak test of V6. In a new setting (instruction tuning on protein tasks), Table 1 compares instruction-tuned TinyLlama 1.1B, OpenLlama-v2 3B and Llama2 7B. The authors read the comparison as showing 'certain scaling laws'. The models come from different families, there are only three of them, and no fit or prediction is made. Scaling is mainly cited as motivation for using mixture-of-experts.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The main conclusion is that SEPIT beats zero-shot, instruction-tuned and sequence-only baselines on the protein benchmark. The 'certain scaling laws' remark is a passing aside in Section 5.2, not part of the paper's conclusion. The authors also say pure LLMs reach only limited performance without protein-language-model prior knowledge.
record.recipe_differences: This is a protein-understanding instruction-tuning and evaluation study, not a language-model pretraining-loss scaling-law experiment. The downstream benchmark and model comparisons differ from the original scaling-law method.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors identify chat-assistant fine-tuning status as relevant to OpenLlama-v2's result. They do not vary scaling-law fitting methods or schedules to test fit dependence.
record.problems: The downstream comparison uses different model families and fine-tuning setups, so scale is not isolated. The paper does not report a quantitative scaling fit or predictive evaluation for this comparison. Individual scores in the supplied flattened table cannot be confidently matched to models and metrics.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows were extracted from Table 1 because its flattened score layout in the supplied text does not support reliable assignment of individual values to the instruction-tuned models and metrics.

untested.parts: Any quantitative predictive relation (fit or extrapolation) between scale or pretraining loss and downstream performance; same-family size sweeps.
No power-law form is fitted for fine-tuning or protein data.

missing.what: OOD protein open-ended scores for TinyLlama vs Llama2. Llama2 is higher on all four metrics (BLEU-2 28.51 vs 22.23; ROUGE-L 41.63 vs 35.39).

Same-pipeline size comparison: SEPIT-TinyLlama (1.8B) vs SEPIT-Llama2 (8B). Gains are modest: BLEU-2 58.43 vs 60.81, accuracy 79.05% vs 79.97%. SEPIT-TinyLlama-MoEs at 1.8B activated parameters nearly matches the 8B model. These are the study's own method variants, so a weak scale signal.
Per-metric Table 1 values for the three instruction-tuned models. The table is readable: 10 metrics in order, with the instruction-tuning rows listed TinyLlama, OpenLlama-v2, Llama2.

record.verdict_notes: This is a protein multimodal instruction-tuning paper, and scaling is peripheral to it. The only scaling evidence is three instruction-tuned models from different families (TinyLlama, OpenLlama-v2, Llama2), so size is confounded with family and with chat tuning. Verdicts should carry little weight. Kaplan et al. is cited only as motivation for mixture-of-experts.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining cross-entropy scaling with parameter count, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of much larger runs from power laws fitted on small runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocations across fixed-compute budgets.
Architecture variations at fixed parameter count.
Power-law behavior in other modalities or training regimes.
The paper compares downstream protein-task performance across model sizes, but does not establish a quantitative predictive relationship with scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of fitted exponents or compute-optimal allocation on parameter counting, schedule, data, or fitting choices.

rows.subject: TinyLlama, OpenLlama-v2, and Llama2 (grouped discussion)
rows.operation_detail: Compared protein-instruction-task performance across instruction-tuned language models of different sizes.

conditions.value: test set of the protein instruction dataset

rows.measure: Protein-task performance across the reported evaluation metrics
rows.value: The authors state that instruction tuning on pure LLMs gives decent protein-understanding capability and demonstrates certain scaling laws.
rows.note: This is the authors' collective qualitative interpretation of the model comparison. Individual table scores are not assigned because the supplied table text does not support a reliable model-to-score mapping.
rows.check: The value is only the authors' qualitative phrase, but Table 1 numbers can be read. Open-ended: TinyLlama 51.16 / OpenLlama-v2 36.19 / Llama2 57.02 BLEU-2, and ROUGE-L 62.31 / 45.53 / 67.78. Closed-set accuracy: 74.09% / 71.77% / 71.68%, which falls with size. The row should be split by task type, with the numbers filled in.

rows.subject: OpenLlama-v2
rows.operation_detail: Compared its protein-task performance with the other instruction-tuned language models.

conditions.value: test set of the protein instruction dataset

rows.value: The authors describe its results as suboptimal and attribute this to its not being specifically fine-tuned for chat-assistant use.
rows.note: The stated explanation points to model and fine-tuning differences as a qualification on interpreting the size comparison.
rows.check: OpenLlama-v2 (3B) scores below TinyLlama (1.1B) on every open-ended and closed-set metric, e.g. BLEU-2 36.19 vs 51.16 and accuracy 71.77% vs 74.09%. Relative to size this is non-monotone, not merely 'partial'. The authors attribute it to OpenLlama-v2 not being chat-tuned.

relationships.condition: Open-ended protein generation, instruction-tuned TinyLlama 1.1B vs Llama2 7B (both chat models)
relationships.reason: Llama2 beats TinyLlama on all open-ended metrics (BLEU-2 57.02 vs 51.16), and also on OOD proteins in Table 6 (28.51 vs 22.23). Only two points, so this is weak support (r1).
relationships.display_finding: Llama2 outperforms TinyLlama on every open-ended metric, including BLEU-2 of 57.02 versus 51.16 and out-of-distribution protein scores of 28.51 versus 22.23, in a two-model comparison.

relationships.reason: The 3B model is worst on all metrics, below the 1.1B model. The ordering depends on the model's prior tuning rather than size alone (r2).
relationships.display_finding: The 3B model scored below the 1.1B model on every metric, with ordering depending on prior tuning.

relationships.condition: Closed-set yes/no protein questions, instruction-tuned pure LLMs
relationships.reason: Accuracy falls with size: 74.09% (1.1B), 71.77% (3B), 71.68% (7B), per Table 1. Model families differ, so this is confounded (r1).
relationships.display_finding: Accuracy declined from 74.09% at 1.1B to 71.77% at 3B and 71.68% at 7B, although the models belonged to different families.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Instruction-tuned pure LLMs on the protein instruction benchmark, as discussed collectively
reader_labels.reason: The authors say this comparison shows certain scaling laws, although they do not provide a clearly assignable quantitative trend here (r1).
